lead: Eigenvalues look like isolated numbers from det(A − λI)=0, but they obey simple bookkeeping rules. Their sum is the trace, their product is the determinant, and powers, inverses and polynomials transform each eigenvalue in the same way. These rules let you check a long calculation in seconds, read eigenvalues of triangular and diagonal matrices by eye, and predict the behaviour of repeated operations such as a Markov chain or a circuit simulated many times. Multiplicities then tell you how many independent eigenvectors are available, which decides whether diagonalization is possible.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for det(A − λI)=0, matrix algebra, and complex numbers.

blocks.text: For an n×n matrix A, tr(A) is the sum of its diagonal entries. List the eigenvalues as λ<sub>1</sub>, …, λ<sub>n</sub>, repeating each eigenvalue according to its algebraic multiplicity, its repeat count as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
tr(A) = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> λ<sub>i</sub>,   det(A) = Π<sub>i=1</sub><sup>n</sup> λ<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: λ<sub>i</sub> are the eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity; tr(A) is the trace; det(A) is the determinant. The formulas hold over real or complex numbers.

blocks.text: A diagonal matrix has eigenvalues equal to its diagonal entries. A triangular matrix also has eigenvalues equal to its diagonal entries; the off-diagonal entries do not change the characteristic polynomial.
Transformed matrices keep the same eigenvectors and change only the eigenvalue:

items: Ak has eigenvalues λik for every positive integer k.
A−1 has eigenvalues 1/λi when det(A) ≠ 0; if det(A)=0, no inverse exists.
p(A) has eigenvalues p(λi) for every polynomial p(t); p(A)=amAm+…+a0I.

blocks.text: These rules do not extend to sums: eigenvalues of A+B are not generally λ<sub>i</sub>(A)+λ<sub>i</sub>(B).

If B=P−1AP, then A and B are similar. They represent the same linear map in different bases (see Chapter 4.4). Their characteristic polynomials are equal: det(B−λI)=det(P−1(A−λI)P)=det(A−λI). So similar matrices have the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities. An eigenvector v of A becomes P−1v for B.
Special matrices force eigenvalues onto known sets. Let H* mean conjugate transpose.

items: Orthogonal Q (QTQ=I) and unitary U (U*U=I): every eigenvalue satisfies |λ|=1, so it lies on the unit circle.
Hermitian H (H*=H) and real symmetric A (AT=A): all eigenvalues are real.
Real skew-symmetric A (AT=−A): every eigenvalue is 0 or purely imaginary, and non-real ones occur in conjugate pairs.
Normal N (N*N=NN*): eigenvectors belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Real symmetric, orthogonal and skew-symmetric matrices are normal.

blocks.text: The real symmetric case is the spectral theorem, developed in Chapter 4.5.

For an eigenvalue λ, the algebraic multiplicity a(λ) is its number of repeats as a root of the characteristic polynomial. The geometric multiplicity g(λ) is the dimension of the null space of A−λI; it counts independent eigenvectors for λ.

blocks.where: g(λ)=dim null(A−λI); a(λ) is the algebraic multiplicity. Equality g(λ)=a(λ) for every eigenvalue is exactly the condition for diagonalizability.

blocks.text: A shortage g(λ)<a(λ) means there are too few independent eigenvectors for that eigenvalue. A repeated eigenvalue can still be diagonalizable when g(λ)=a(λ).

Distinct eigenvalues always give independent eigenvectors. One proof: take a shortest relation c<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub>+…+c<sub>m</sub>v<sub>m</sub>=0 with distinct λ<sub>i</sub> and nonzero c<sub>i</sub>. Apply A−λ<sub>m</sub>I. The last term dies, leaving a shorter relation among v<sub>1</sub>,…,v<sub>m−1</sub>, a contradiction.

figure.caption: For eigenvalues 2 and 5, the sum is the trace, the product is the determinant, and powers, inverses and polynomials act on each eigenvalue.

spec.aria: A tree of eigenvalue properties: sum is trace, product is determinant, powers, inverses and polynomials transform each eigenvalue.

examples.question: A 2×2 matrix A has eigenvalues 2 and 5. Find tr(A), det(A), the eigenvalues of A², the eigenvalues of A⁻¹, and the eigenvalues of p(A) for p(t)=t²−3t+1.
steps: Determinant = product with multiplicity: 2×5=10. Since 10 ≠ 0, A⁻¹ exists.
examples.answer: The trace is 7, the determinant is 10; A² has eigenvalues 4 and 25; A⁻¹ has eigenvalues 0.5 and 0.2; p(A) has eigenvalues −1 and 11.
examples.check:
print(2+5)
print(2*5)
print(2**2)
print(5**2)
print(1/2)
print(1/5)
print(2**2 - 3*2 + 1)
print(5**2 - 3*5 + 1)

traps: Trace and determinant give only the sum and product of eigenvalues, not the individual eigenvalues, unless the matrix is 2×2 or you have extra information.
Eigenvalues of A+B are not generally the sums of eigenvalues of A and B; test with two simple 2×2 matrices.
For A<sup>k</sup> and p(A), the eigenvalues become λ<sup>k</sup> and p(λ), but the eigenvectors stay the same; do not replace eigenvectors by powers.
A<sup>−1</sup> has eigenvalues 1/λ only when det(A) ≠ 0; a zero eigenvalue means no inverse.
A repeated eigenvalue does not automatically mean failure of diagonalization; check whether geometric multiplicity equals algebraic multiplicity.

quiz.q: State the trace and determinant formulas for eigenvalues.
quiz.a: tr(A)=Σλ<sub>i</sub> and det(A)=Πλ<sub>i</sub>, with each eigenvalue repeated by algebraic multiplicity.

quiz.q: Why do A and P<sup>−1</sup>AP have the same eigenvalues?
quiz.a: det(P<sup>−1</sup>AP−λI)=det(P<sup>−1</sup>(A−λI)P)=det(A−λI). The characteristic polynomials are equal, so their roots are equal.

quiz.q: A 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues −1, 2, 4. Find tr(A), det(A), and the eigenvalues of A² and A⁻¹.
A 3×3 real matrix has eigenvalues 1, i, −i. What type of matrix can it be? Explain.
quiz.a: It can be orthogonal: all eigenvalues have modulus 1 and non-real eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. It cannot be real symmetric, which needs real eigenvalues, or real skew-symmetric, whose eigenvalues are 0 or purely imaginary.

quiz.q: A matrix has eigenvalue 3 with algebraic multiplicity 3 and geometric multiplicity 1. Is it diagonalizable? How many independent eigenvectors belong to λ=3?
quiz.a: No. It has only one independent eigenvector for λ=3, but three are needed from that eigenvalue alone to reach a full basis.

quiz.q: Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors. What fails for repeated eigenvalues?
quiz.a: The independence proof uses distinct λ<sub>i</sub>. With repeats, the null spaces can be too small; the geometric multiplicity may be less than the algebraic multiplicity.

quiz.q: A real 3×3 skew-symmetric matrix A has what possible eigenvalues and trace?
quiz.a: Eigenvalues are 0 or purely imaginary, in conjugate pairs. In odd dimension at least one eigenvalue is 0. The trace equals the sum of eigenvalues, so tr(A)=0, also because the diagonal entries are 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. These bookkeeping rules underpin Google's PageRank (dominant eigenvalue), vibration analysis (natural frequencies), and stability of control systems (eigenvalues in the left half-plane). In data science, covariance eigenvalues drive PCA; in graph mining, graph spectra reveal communities. Search next for spectral theorem, Perron-Frobenius theorem, and eigenvalue sensitivity.
